metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Cherry Hills Village, CO
metaDescription: Cherry Hills Village is a small, fully residential Arapahoe County enclave. See how old ranch-era mineral severances still apply under one of Denver's wealthiest suburbs.
heroLead: Cherry Hills Village is one of the smaller, more affluent residential enclaves in Arapahoe County, built on ground that was ranchland well into the 20th century, and mineral rights here trace back to that earlier chapter regardless of what's since been built above them.
intro: A mineral interest connected to a Cherry Hills Village legal description almost always predates the large residential estates that define the area today. The severance happened when the land was still agricultural, and the interest has passed through inheritance since — often independently of whoever currently owns the surface home, since the two ownership chains split apart generations ago.

It's worth being direct about that split: the value of a village mineral interest today has almost nothing to do with the value of the surface real estate sitting above it. Two owners can hold interests of very different worth even in adjoining sections, depending on the exact wording of the original severance and where the tract falls relative to any pooled unit.

sections.heading: No realistic surface drilling prospect
paragraphs: Given the density and value of surface development in this area, there's essentially no chance of a well being sited within the village itself. Any theoretical development of the minerals beneath it would require a directional well drilled from well outside the area, which is a long, uncertain path rather than an active prospect.

sections.heading: An interest most owners don't know they hold
paragraphs: Because the mineral estate here was typically severed a century or more ago, current descendants are often surprised to learn they hold anything at all — it usually surfaces through a probate filing, an old family document, or a distant relative's estate settlement. Confirming the interest starts with the Arapahoe County Clerk and Recorder's deed and probate index.

sections.heading: Why we still make offers on low-probability interests
paragraphs: Even with a low probability of near-term development, a mineral interest retains some value simply because it's a real, transferable legal asset. We price these interests conservatively against realistic odds, but we don't treat low probability as zero value, and we're comfortable evaluating interests that most owners assume aren't worth pursuing.

faqs.question: Do I actually own something if I've never heard of a mineral interest before?
faqs.answer: Possibly. Old ranch-era severances are common in this area and often surface unexpectedly through probate. We can search county records to confirm.

faqs.question: Could my minerals ever actually be drilled?
faqs.answer: It's unlikely given the density of development, though not impossible in theory through directional drilling from outside the area. We price offers against that realistic low probability.

faqs.question: Is it worth selling a low-probability interest instead of just holding it?
faqs.answer: Often yes, since a sale converts an indefinite, uncertain holding into a known amount today.

faqs.question: What does the county record show about my interest?
faqs.answer: Typically the original severance deed, any subsequent assignments, and the current chain of inheritance. We can pull and interpret this record as part of any evaluation.
